extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, creative-writing students, and workshop participants working on openings/first pages
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and criteria for crafting effective first pages/openings of fiction, with emphasis on point of view, narrative voice, and how much information to provide. Includes critiques of example openings to illustrate pitfalls and best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: default omniscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Omniscience without plan, passion, or purpose — a loose, distorted narrative filter that muddies perspective and leaves the reader unclear whose experience they're getting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'default omniscience' where narration drifts between characters' minds and an impersonal narrator with no deliberate organizing principle. The article calls this 'the deadliest first-page sin' and illustrates with passages that oscillate between Hank's, Lila's, and a generalized view of all adolescents, producing information rather than inhabitable experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: NO POINT OF VIEW = NO STORY
rubrics_metrics.description: A story/novel must be bound by a specific, consistent, and rigorously controlled viewpoint; without an established POV there is no story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat point of view as fundamental (as important as tense or diction). If a viewpoint isn't properly established, line-editing won't fix deep problems. Use the chosen POV as the organizing principle for everything the reader sees.

rubrics_metrics.name: subjectivity filter / render experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction must render human experience through subjectivity: events should be conveyed insofar as characters feel and react to them, i.e., through a nervous-system-based filter (a character or an omniscient narrator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experiences aren't passed through a subjective filter, the result is information, not experience. Ensure sensations, thoughts, and reactions are filtered through a realized consciousness to make the reader inhabit the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: create and commit to a narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator is an emissary inside the story who must be consciously created and embedded; authors must not confuse narrator with author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should 'create' the narrator and embed that narrator into character psyches as needed. The narrator should mediate between author and story; don't let the authorial presence intrude or second-guess the narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid author intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorial intrusions—when the author's voice/knowledge displaces the narrator—violate POV and dissolve the fictional dream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the author's outside perspective out of scenes; let the narrator's consciousness determine what is shown and how. Intrusions turn experience back into information and break reader immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: consistency in POV (no head-hopping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a solid, consistent POV; avoid subtle and not-so-subtle shifts that leave readers unclear whose experience they're getting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for shifts even within a paragraph (e.g., sentence-by-sentence jumps between characters' thoughts). If you need multiple perspectives, establish transitions deliberately (new sections/chapters or clear markers) and do so consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: establish POV early
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly establish whose viewpoint is in control at the start so there is a filter in place from which all experience is presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed the narrator into the character's psyche early so lapses are impossible. Lack of an early established filter leads to confusing objective statements that readers interpret as omniscient judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: choose POV knowingly (omniscient allowed if deliberate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omniscient narration and multiple perspectives can work, but only if used deliberately and with authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't default into omniscience; if you opt for omniscient voice, do so with a plan and maintain its scope and purpose. Conversely, single-character POVs should be fully inhabited and consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid passive constructions that detach viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive or distancing constructions can locate viewpoint beyond the character's immediate subjective experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active, sensory, and immediate phrasing that could plausibly come from the character's consciousness (e.g., 'Aidan yawned and shifted in his seat' vs. 'It was the longest plane trip that Aidan had ever been on').

rubrics_metrics.name: use diction appropriate to the character's psyche
rubrics_metrics.description: Word choice should match the character's age, education, and mental state; mismatched diction yanks readers out of the character's perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language that feels adult, clinical, or anachronistic for the character (e.g., 'dietary adjustment' for an eight-year-old). Render sensations and reactions in terms the character would experience and articulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: dramatization versus summary/exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide early whether to dramatize events or summarize them; this choice interacts with tense, diction, and POV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat dramatization/summary as part of the POV decision. Prefer dramatized scenes that put readers with the character when you want immersion; use summary sparingly and intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: first page should evoke character (not just setting/description)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong first page should give readers access to the characters whose dramas they'll experience, not merely describe weather or spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide information that helps readers answer key questions (who is this person, what is her relation to others, what is at stake). Avoid openings that supply rich sensory description but leave character and situation vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: first page should raise correct expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The first page forges a tacit understanding between reader and author about voice, technique, and what to expect from the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opening to signal tense, POV, voice and style (first-person? omniscient? lyric? epic?). Meet those expectations or deliberately subvert them; otherwise readers feel misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: front-load the scene/action when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the central action or inciting detail early enough to orient reader interest and raise relevant stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a detail (e.g., an incoming phone call) is the focus, lead with it ('They were watching the fireworks when Kate's phone vibrated.') so readers enter with the right curiosity and tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: balance information vs. questions: generosity over false suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide enough information for readers to understand the scene and form meaningful questions, instead of withholding so much that the reader asks 'What am I reading?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'false suspense'—confusion caused by withholding essentials. Confident writers tend toward generosity: give the reader what they need to be curious about consequences rather than context.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid introducing too many names/characters/unearned flashbacks early
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing multiple named people and emotional backstory on the first page can overwhelm readers and dilute present-moment tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground readers in the main character/POV and present action before layering in past events or additional characters; avoid unearned emotional detail and abrupt flashbacks that ask readers to care prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: use a cunningly chosen first sentence to set expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific, well-chosen opening sentence can thrust readers into the crux of the story and raise curiosity and tension right away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Front-load a telling detail that signals stakes or conflict (e.g., 'Kate was watching the fireworks display with her fiancé when the casting director called.'). Avoid vague, meandering leads that create boredom rather than intrigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: nothing should reach the reader that hasn't passed through the POV filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Every idea, observation, and judgment in the narrative should logically come from the established narrator's perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit prose to ensure descriptions, evaluations, and background align with the narrator's knowledge and sensibility. If an omniscient stance is used, justify it; otherwise keep details within the narrator's plausible awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: point of view is as fundamental as tense or diction
rubrics_metrics.description: POV is a foundational choice that shapes the story and cannot be treated as incidental or patched on later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide POV early in the writing process; changing it later is like trying to add a canvas to a finished painting. Make POV the organizing principle for style, voice, and what information is disclosed.
